content: Learned helplessness is a psychological condition in which an individual, whether human or animal, comes to believe that they are powerless in a specific situation. This belief arises from the perception that they have no control over their circumstances and that any action they take will be futile. Consequently, the individual remains passive in the face of unpleasant, harmful, or damaging situations, even when they actually possess the ability to change their circumstances. The theory of learned helplessness posits that depression can result from a perceived lack of control over life events. This perception often stems from prior exposure to negative events that were either truly or seemingly uncontrollable. Learned helplessness is a well-established concept in psychology and has been demonstrated in both laboratory and real-world settings. In laboratory experiments, learned helplessness has been observed in animals subjected to inescapable punishment, such as electrical shocks. For example, in a seminal experiment by Martin Seligman and Steve Maier, dogs were divided into three groups. Group 1 dogs were placed in harnesses for a period of time and then released without experiencing shocks. Group 2 dogs were given shocks that they could terminate by pressing a lever. Group 3 dogs, however, were yoked to Group 2 dogs and received shocks of identical intensity and duration, but their lever had no effect. For Group 3 dogs, the shocks appeared random and inescapable because their cessation depended on the actions of their paired Group 2 dogs. When later tested in a shuttle-box apparatus, where dogs could escape shocks by jumping over a low partition, Group 3 dogs—having learned that their actions were ineffective—remained passive. They lay down, whined, and did not attempt to escape, even though they could have avoided the shocks. This behavior mirrored symptoms of chronic clinical depression. In contrast, Group 1 and Group 2 dogs quickly recovered and adapted to the new situation. Further experiments ruled out the possibility that Group 3 dogs had learned some interfering behavior during their initial exposure to inescapable shocks. For instance, when Group 3 dogs were immobilized with a paralyzing drug (curare) during the initial phase and then tested in the shuttle-box, they still exhibited the same helpless response. Similar results were observed in experiments with other animals, consistently showing that the strongest predictor of a depressive response was the lack of control over negative stimuli. Learned helplessness has also been demonstrated in humans. For example, in one study, infants were placed in cribs with sensory pillows. In one group, the infants could control the movement of a mobile by moving their heads, while in another group, the mobile's movement was independent of the infants' actions. When later given the opportunity to control the mobile, infants from the second group, who had previously learned that their actions had no effect, did not attempt to exert control. This lack of agency persisted, reflecting the aftereffects of their earlier experience of helplessness. Similarly, in experiments involving adults performing mental tasks in the presence of distracting noise, individuals who had a switch to turn off the noise performed better, even if they rarely used the switch. The mere awareness of having control over the noise was enough to mitigate its distracting effects. Not all individuals or animals exposed to uncontrollable situations develop learned helplessness. In Seligman's experiments, approximately one-third of the dogs did not become helpless, despite their prior experiences. These dogs managed to find ways to escape the unpleasant situation. In humans, this resilience has been linked to an optimistic explanatory style, where individuals view problems as external, specific, and temporary, rather than personal, pervasive, or permanent. The concept of learned helplessness has also been extended beyond psychology to the realm of social action. Sociologist Harrison White suggested that organizations or nations could experience learned helplessness when recurrent failures in the past lead to a failure to act in the present, even when action is possible. This broader application highlights the pervasive impact of learned helplessness on both individual and collective behavior.
